raw_response:
I’m still doing wheat-maize on the 20 mu. That’s what I know, and on land like ours it is the safest way to keep grain coming in. I don’t read those technical things, so I mostly go by what I’ve seen on my own fields and what the neighbors do. Last year wheat did alright with a decent base fertilizer and two topdressings, and maize followed well when we planted quickly after harvest. Money matters, and with some people working outside, our labor is not all free at the right time, so I won’t do anything too fancy this year. I’ll keep fertilizer at a medium level, not the highest, because prices are not low, but I also don’t want the crop to turn weak and lose yield. Since I have well water, I will save irrigation for the key times, especially for wheat, and for maize only if summer rain is not enough.

For wheat, I’ll sow around the usual October time with improved seed that people nearby use, because it emerges evenly and gives steadier yield than saved seed. I’ll put most fertilizer before sowing, then add more when the wheat starts growing strong in spring. For maize, the main thing is speed after wheat harvest. We don’t have much time between the two crops, so I’ll use simple rotary tillage or even just quick field preparation and plant right away. Maize usually gets enough rain here, but if the weather turns dry and the leaves roll, I’ll irrigate once or twice. I’m trying to keep costs in hand while still making sure both crops have enough input to avoid a bad year.
